narration:
Every queue is a small government. It has a constitution — usually unwritten. One person, one place. No proxies after a certain hour. The elderly and the pregnant may be waved forward by common consent. It has enforcement, too: the cough, the stare, the muttered escalation. And it has diplomacy — the negotiated absence. "I'm just going to move my car, this is my spot." Above all, it has a theory of fairness so widely shared that no one even thinks of it as a theory.

This is why queue-jumping enrages us out of all proportion to its cost. Thirty seconds of delay from a slow cashier? Forgiven without a second thought. But those same thirty seconds, taken by a man sliding in near the front — that feels like an act of violence. Because it isn't a theft of time. It's a repudiation of the constitution. He has declared, in front of everyone, that the government does not exist for him. And every person in that queue feels the insult personally — because each of them has been paying taxes to that government since the moment they arrived. Standing, when they could have pushed. Waiting, when they could have schemed.

Notice, too, how quickly the state forms. Three people at a bus stop are just a crowd. But four are a queue — and the fourth arrival can usually reconstruct the order of the first three without even asking. We assemble these micro-nations dozens of times a day. We ratify their laws simply by standing still. And we dissolve them without ceremony, the moment the bus arrives. No flags. No anthems. And yet I have seen men in expensive suits — men who negotiate for a living, men who would call patriotism sentimental — go visibly red defending the sovereignty of a sandwich line.

The queue is proof of something we rarely credit ourselves with: that ordinary people, unsupervised, will build fairness out of nothing but shared standing and mutual watching — and will pay real costs to maintain it. But it is also proof of the fragility underneath. One unpunished violation, and the constitution wobbles. Two, and men who waited politely for twenty minutes begin edging forward — because no one keeps paying taxes to a government that has stopped existing. Order of this kind is not a possession. It is a practice. Renewed by every single person who joins the end of the line, when no one would have stopped them doing otherwise.
